parsed_answer.content: Test-Driven Development (TDD) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) using Cucumber represent two distinct evolutionary tiers of software design driven by executable specifications. While TDD focuses on the developer-centric implementation of technical contracts, classes, and methods via the red-green-refactor cycle, BDD scales this philosophy outward to bridge the communication chasm between business stakeholders, QA, and developers. BDD forces teams to define system behavior in a ubiquitous, human-readable language using the Gherkin syntax (Given-When-Then), which Cucumber then parses and maps directly to automated step definitions. In enterprise Java architectures, mastering both paradigms ensures that low-level components are meticulously tested for invariants and edge cases, while high-level system workflows align precisely with domain-driven design requirements.

items: TDD strictly follows the Red-Green-Refactor loop: write a failing unit test, write the minimal production code to make it pass, and then refactor the structure without changing behavior.
BDD leverages Cucumber to translate plain-text Gherkin scenarios into Java methods via Regular Expressions or Cucumber Expressions, executing acceptance tests against the application context.

Under the hood, Cucumber scans feature files, matches step annotations (@Given, @When, @Then), and invokes glue code that typically drives Spring Boot integration tests or Selenium/Playwright browser drivers.

parsed_answer.content: A common anti-pattern in BDD is writing Cucumber feature files that mirror low-level technical implementation details rather than business capabilities. BDD is not just 'TDD in English'; writing brittle step definitions that tightly couple Gherkin scripts to UI element IDs leads to high maintenance overhead. Keep Cucumber tests focused on acceptance-level business logic, and rely on TDD for underlying algorithmic and domain-model validation.
